name: Medial meniscus — posterior horn
description: Largest third of the medial meniscus, always larger than the anterior horn on sagittal images, attached peripherally to the posteromedial capsule (the ramp region) and narrowing centrally into the posterior root. The commonest site of medial tears; sagittal images show it best.
variants_pitfalls: Ramp lesion (about 9–42% of ACL reconstructions): a peripheral longitudinal tear at the capsular attachment that MRI often misses (pooled sensitivity 71%). Look for fluid completely separating horn and capsule; a posteromedial tibial bone bruise is a prompt.

Without ACL injury or a bone bruise, a thin fluid line between horn and capsule is not a ramp lesion: it was present in 35% of consecutive knees, most without an ACL tear (recesses, gastrocnemius bursa, vascular rim).

Signal that does not reach a surface is degeneration, or vascular in children (66% of asymptomatic children). Call a tear when it reaches the surface on 2 or more images; on one image it is a possible tear.
A posterior horn smaller than the anterior horn, blunted or missing means a displaced fragment (notch, double PCL, flipped anteriorly) or prior meniscectomy.
Degenerative tears are common with age (19–56% over 50, most painless); report them, but do not assume they explain symptoms.
